details:
ASTRION CARE is an astronaut health monitoring and early warning platform developed to address the challenges of maintaining crew health during long-duration space missions. Astronauts experience several health risks due to microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, disrupted sleep cycles, and changing physical conditions. Gradual health changes may go unnoticed when monitoring relies only on individual readings or periodic observations.

Our solution introduces a personalized baseline-based monitoring approach. Each astronaut has an individual health profile built from regular health check-ins and available measurements. The application collects health information such as heart rate, sleep duration, exercise activity, mood, and reported symptoms. Current readings are compared against the astronaut's historical patterns to identify unusual changes and combinations of indicators.

The system uses rule-based trend analysis and data-quality validation to identify potentially concerning patterns. It provides understandable health alerts, explanations, recommendations, and historical visualizations through an interactive dashboard. A three-level alert approach can be used to communicate different levels of attention, provided the corresponding alert rules are implemented in the prototype.

ASTRION CARE is designed with offline accessibility in mind. Local browser storage allows health records to remain accessible without continuous internet connectivity, making the approach suitable for isolated mission environments.

The prototype is developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with browser LocalStorage for local records and Chart.js for health-trend visualization. The application is deployed as a web-based prototype. Simulated astronaut profiles and sample health readings support demonstration and testing without requiring real astronaut medical data or spacecraft hardware.

The project considers data reliability, missing measurements, false alerts, privacy, and the limitations of simulated data. It is designed as a health decision-support tool rather than a medical diagnostic system, with real-world deployment requiring clinical validation, secure infrastructure, and qualified medical supervision.

Our goal is to improve early awareness of personal health changes, support structured self-monitoring, and make health information easier to understand and communicate during space missions. The underlying personalized monitoring approach could also be adapted for other isolated environments, including submarines, polar research stations, and remote field operations.
